0.title: Lamentations: Great Is Your Faithfulness
0.overview:
Lamentations is a book of tears. In about 586 BC the army of Babylon broke through the walls of Jerusalem after a long siege, burned the house of the LORD, the king's palace and every great house in the city, and took the people into exile (2 Kgs 25:8-10). Lamentations is what God's people said, and prayed, standing in the ashes.

It is five poems, one to a chapter. The book does not name its author. It has long been associated with Jeremiah, who warned for forty years that this day would come and wept over his people (Jer 9:1), and the voice of chapter 3 sounds very like his. The Greek Old Testament adds a preface naming Jeremiah; the Hebrew has none, and the poems speak for the whole nation.

In Hebrew, chapters 1, 2 and 4 are acrostics: twenty-two verses beginning with the twenty-two letters of the alphabet in order. Chapter 3 does the same in sets of three, which is why it has sixty-six verses. Chapter 5 has twenty-two verses but lets go of the alphabet. (In chapters 2 to 4 the letters ayin and pe swap places.) Grief is given the most ordered shape the poet has, as if even this sorrow can be brought before God from A to Z.

Several voices speak: a narrator describing the ruined city, Jerusalem herself as a widow with no one to comfort her (chapter 1), a single man broken by God to whom hope returns (chapter 3), and the whole community praying together (chapter 5).

The book is honest about three things at once. First, the LORD did this; Babylon was only the instrument: The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago (2:17). Second, he was right to do it. For generations his prophets were mocked until there was no remedy (2 Chr 36:16), and Jerusalem confesses, The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word (1:18). Third, it hurts terribly, and the book says so without holding back. (That verdict falls on a nation after centuries of warning, not on every sorrow a reader carries; chapter 3 takes up that question.)

At the centre of the book comes the turn. A man at the end of his strength says But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness (3:21-23). What has changed is what he remembers about God, who does not afflict from his heart (3:33).

Lamentations teaches God's people how to grieve. Lament is not unbelief. It is faith that still speaks to God in the dark: confessing sin, pouring out the heart like water (2:19), asking him to look, and holding on to his character when his hand is heavy. It gives words to those who have lost homes, health, children or hope, naming horrors survivors often cannot speak of. It teaches the church to sit with the grieving without rushing them: weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). And it refuses to hurry to a happy ending. Its last line is a question (5:22).

That question is answered in Jesus Christ. Jerusalem had no comforter (1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21); God keeps his promise of comfort as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort (2 Cor 1:3-4). Jesus himself saw the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41). The man of chapter 3, mocked and thrown into the pit, points to the one who suffered all of it without any sin of his own. The cup of wrath Jerusalem drank for her sins, Christ drank for the sins of others, and he truly cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). Because he was forsaken, those who belong to him never will be. Lamentations begins with tears on a widow's cheeks that no one wipes away; the Bible closes with the promise that God will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Rev 21:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — How Lonely Sits the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens with a cry over the city that was full of people, now a widow with none to comfort her (vv. 1–2). Judah is in exile and the pilgrim roads mourn (vv. 3–4); the cause is named, and it is not Babylon: the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions (v. 5). Her princes flee and she remembers what was hers (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The first cause of Jerusalem's ruin is not Babylon's strength but the LORD's just response to her sin.

verseByVerse.quote: How lonely sits the city that was full of people! How like a widow has she become, she who was great among the nations! She who was a princess among the provinces has become a slave. She weeps bitterly in the night, with tears on her cheeks; among all her lovers she has none to comfort her; all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book opens with an exclamation, not an explanation. In the summer of about 586 BC the Babylonian commander burned the house of the LORD, the king's palace and every great house in Jerusalem, and broke down its walls (2 Kgs 25:8-10). The people who once crowded the streets have been marched away. The poet stands in the ash and can only say: How.

Three pictures, each a reversal. Full of people, now lonely. Great among the nations, now a widow. A princess, now a slave. The city sits, which is how mourners sat, on the ground with nowhere left to go.

The widow is the sharpest of the three. In Israel a widow had lost her protector, her provider and her standing. But Jerusalem's husband has not died. The LORD is alive. She is a widow because the one who loved her has withdrawn his presence after she left him for others. That is what makes this loneliness so deep: it is the loneliness of a people whose God has stepped back.

Grief is worst at night, when there is nothing to do but feel it. One detail stays: tears on her cheeks. The tears are still there because no one has wiped them away.

Her lovers are the nations and their gods she ran after instead of the LORD: Egypt, Assyria and the alliances Jeremiah had warned would fail her (Jer 2:36-37; 4:30). When the siege came, none of them came. The friends she had trusted instead of God turned out to be enemies.

Here, too, the refrain of the chapter is heard for the first time: none to comfort her. It will come back four more times (vv. 9, 16, 17, 21). That word is the ache at the centre of this whole chapter, and the chapter does not hurry past it. Whatever you are grieving, the question it presses is the right one: who is going to comfort me?

Lamentations does not reach the answer, but the answer was already given to exactly this woman. Through Isaiah God had said, for this very ruin, Comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isa 40:1), and the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. For your Maker is your husband (Isa 54:4-5). And the end of the Bible answers it: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes (Rev 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: The book's Hebrew title is its first word, ekah, "How!" Jewish communities still read it on the ninth of Ab, the fast that mourns the destruction of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah has gone into exile because of affliction and hard servitude; she dwells now among the nations, but finds no resting place; her pursuers have all overtaken her in the midst of her distress. The roads to Zion mourn, for none come to the festival; all her gates are desolate; her priests groan; her virgins have been afflicted, and she herself suffers bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that the phrase because of affliction can also be rendered "under affliction." Either way, the picture is of a people driven out bent low, going into exile already broken by the siege.

Moses had said exactly this would happen if Israel broke the covenant: among these nations you shall find no respite, and there shall be no resting place for the sole of your foot (Deut 28:65). The curses written down centuries earlier are being read out in the streets of Jerusalem.

Where the ESV reads in the midst of her distress, its note gives "in the narrow passes" as an alternative: the image of fugitives caught in a gorge with no way out. That is precisely what happened to the king. Zedekiah fled the city by night, and the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho (Jer 39:5).

Picture the roads up to Jerusalem at Passover or the Feast of Booths: families walking for days, singing as they climbed, the gates choked with crowds. I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!" (Ps 122:1). Now the roads are empty, and the poet says the roads themselves are in mourning.

The gates where business was done and justice given are deserted. The priests have nothing to offer. The young women who once danced at the feasts have been afflicted; the ESV notes that the Septuagint and Old Latin read "dragged away".

This city had grown used to the festivals and assumed they would always be there. It is possible to lose the delight of God's gathered people long before the building is burned, and only notice what it was when the road is empty.

verseByVerse.quote: Her foes have become the head; her enemies prosper, because the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions; her children have gone away, captives before the foe. From the daughter of Zion all her majesty has departed. Her princes have become like deer that find no pasture; they fled without strength before the pursuer. Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and wandering all the precious things that were hers from days of old. When her people fell into the hand of the foe, and there was none to help her, her foes gloated over her; they mocked at her downfall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her foes have become the head is another covenant curse read aloud: He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail (Deut 28:44).

Then, in the middle of the verse, the reason, and it is the theological backbone of the whole book. The natural thing to say after a disaster is that the bigger army won. Lamentations will not say that. Babylon was the rod; the LORD held it, because of the multitude of her transgressions: not one sin but generations of idolatry, injustice and refusal to listen (Jer 7:13).

That is hard to hear. But it is also the only ground for hope. If Babylon's power were the last word, there would be nothing to pray for. If the LORD did this, then the LORD can be spoken to, and the LORD can undo it.

The daughter of Zion is the city pictured as a young woman, a name that runs all through this book. Her princes are like starving deer, too weak to outrun anything. Again the history stands behind the poetry: when the wall was breached, the king and his soldiers fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king's garden (Jer 39:4). The men who were supposed to protect the people were the first out of the gate.

Memory is one of the cruellest parts of suffering. The worst nights are the ones when you remember what used to be: the house, the marriage, the health, the church, the child. A psalmist knew it: These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God (Ps 42:4).

The poem does not yet go further than that. But keep your finger in this page, because in chapter 3 the same man who says My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me goes on: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope (3:20-21). The cure for a memory that drags you down is not to stop remembering; it is to remember something more: the steadfast love of the LORD, which is older than the good days and outlasts the bad ones.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem sinned grievously and became filthy, never thinking where her path led (vv. 8–9). Enemies enter the sanctuary and the people barter treasures for bread (vv. 10–11), and twice the city breaks in with a prayer that the LORD would look (vv. 9, 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin blinds a people to its own future, but even in the ruin the first words spoken are addressed to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Jerusalem sinned grievously; therefore she became filthy; all who honored her despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; she herself groans and turns her face away. Her uncleanness was in her skirts; she took no thought of her future; therefore her fall is terrible; she has no comforter. "O LORD, behold my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator uses no softening and no euphemism. Sin is not only guilt before a judge. It is defilement. It makes a person and a people unclean, and it cannot be hidden forever.

They have seen her nakedness. Jeremiah had used this picture of public shame for the city that played the harlot with other gods: I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen (Jer 13:26). The nations who once admired Jerusalem now see what she really is.

This is a picture of a nation's shame for its own unfaithfulness. It is never a word against anyone who has been stripped, exposed or abused by another person: that shame belongs to the one who did it, and the abused should seek safety and help at once. God's heart toward such victims is plain in 5:11, where their suffering is written into his book as an outrage.

And she turns her face away, which is what shame does. It has done it since the garden, where the first couple saw that they were naked and hid from God (Gen 3:7-10). The gospel's answer to exposed shame is not a better hiding place. It is clothing from someone else: white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen (Rev 3:18), and Christ was stripped at the cross so that we might be covered.

She took no thought of her future. The ESV notes that future can be rendered "end" — she did not think about where it would end. Moses had grieved over exactly this: If they were wise, they would understand this; they would discern their latter end! (Deut 32:29).

That is how sin works in every life. It is very good at the next five minutes and has nothing to say about the next five years. So it is wise to ask of any road, where does this end? But the strength to turn off it is not ours alone: the God who confronts Jerusalem here is the God who promised to put his Spirit within his people and cause them to walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27).

Then, for the first time, the city speaks, and her first words are a prayer: O LORD, behold my affliction. She has no comforter among the nations, so she turns to the only one left. Her pain has found the right address.

verseByVerse.quote: The enemy has stretched out his hands over all her precious things; for she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, those whom you forbade to enter your congregation. All her people groan as they search for bread; they trade their treasures for food to revive their strength. "Look, O LORD, and see, for I am despised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worst thing is not the looting of gold. It is who is standing where. The law had barred certain peoples from the assembly of the LORD (Deut 23:3), and the holy place itself was closed to all but the priests. Now pagan soldiers are walking into the holy place and carrying out its vessels.

The description turns into prayer mid-sentence, those whom you forbade: Lord, you made the rule; look who is in your house.

There is a deep irony here that the gospel fills out. The nations did come into God's house, but in a way no one in Jerusalem could have imagined. Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19-21), and through that temple outsiders are brought in, not as invaders but as guests: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13).

The siege had ended in famine: the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land (Jer 52:6). Heirlooms, jewellery, the family's savings: all handed over for a loaf.

The treasures Jerusalem had trusted turned out to be worth one meal.

Twice now the city has asked God simply to look. It is the most basic prayer there is: not yet asking him to fix it, only asking him to see. And he does. You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle (Ps 56:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Is It Nothing to You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem speaks for herself, stopping the passers-by (v. 12), tracing every blow to the LORD's hand (vv. 13–15), and coming back to the loss that hurts most: no comforter (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Zion's sorrow was the LORD's anger against her own sin; the sorrow of Christ, which these words have long been used to describe, was the LORD's anger against ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which was brought upon me, which the LORD inflicted on the day of his fierce anger. "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend; he spread a net for my feet; he turned me back; he has left me stunned, faint all the day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the city herself stands by the roadside and calls to travellers walking past a catastrophe and carrying on with their day. Her question has a plain first meaning, and it matters. Suffering is lonelier when others treat it as background. There is a sin of the passer-by: to see someone's ruin and feel nothing. The church is meant to be the place where no one's sorrow is nothing to anyone (2 Cor 1:4).

But Christians have long heard these words at the foot of the cross, and there is good reason for it. At Golgotha, those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Matt 27:39). There was a man by the road outside Jerusalem who suffered on the day of his fierce anger.

Yet look at the difference, because it is the whole gospel. Jerusalem's sorrow came for the multitude of her transgressions (v. 5); she says so herself (v. 18). Christ had none. He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities (Isa 53:5). Jerusalem drank the cup of wrath for her own sin. Jesus drank it for ours. When you ask whether there is any sorrow like his sorrow, the answer is no, because his was the only sorrow ever borne entirely for someone else.

Four pictures, and he is the subject of every one. Fire from above. A hunter's net. A traveller turned back on the road. A body left stunned and fainting.

Jeremiah once said God's word was a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jer 20:9). The city refused that fire, so it received the other kind. The word of God will burn in you one way or the other: as a message you cannot keep in, or as a judgment you cannot keep out.

verseByVerse.quote: "My transgressions were bound into a yoke; by his hand they were fastened together; they were set upon my neck; he caused my strength to fail; the Lord gave me into the hands of those whom I cannot withstand. "The Lord rejected all my mighty men in my midst; he summoned an assembly against me to crush my young men; the Lord has trodden as in a winepress the virgin daughter of Judah. "For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears; for a comforter is far from me, one to revive my spirit; my children are desolate, for the enemy has prevailed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that "The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain" in the first line, but the picture it gives is clear enough. Each sin was like a strap. One by one they were tied together into a yoke, and the yoke was laid on her neck until she could not stand up under it.

That is how sin feels when it is finally felt. Nobody notices one strap, but they were being fastened together, and one day the whole weight arrives at once. Then hear another yoke: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt 11:28-30). Jesus does not invite people with no yoke. He invites people bent double under the one they tied themselves, and offers to exchange it.

God has summoned an assembly: not worshippers for a feast but an army for slaughter.

As in a winepress. Grapes were trampled by foot until the juice ran red. It is a terrible image of judgment, and the New Testament keeps it for the end of history: the great winepress of the wrath of God (Rev 14:19). What Judah felt in 586 BC was a foretaste of a day still to come for the whole world, which is why the refuge from that day is not a strong city but a Saviour.

She names exactly what she needs: not an explanation or a lecture, but someone to come near and revive my spirit.

That is the hunger Jesus answered on the night before he died: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever... I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you (John 14:16, 18). The comforter that was far from Jerusalem has come near in the Son, and dwells in his people by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — The LORD Is in the Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion stretches out her hands and none comforts her (v. 17). She confesses The LORD is in the right (v. 18), pours out her anguish (vv. 19–20), asks God to bring the same day on her enemies, and ends with no answer (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief that confesses God is right can still pour itself out to him, and ask him for justice.

verseByVerse.quote: Zion stretches out her hands, but there is none to comfort her; the LORD has commanded against Jacob that his neighbors should be his foes; Jerusalem has become a filthy thing among them. "The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word; but hear, all you peoples, and see my suffering; my young women and my young men have gone into captivity. "I called to my lovers, but they deceived me; my priests and elders perished in the city, while they sought food to revive their strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator breaks in for a single verse, like a camera pulling back. Zion's hands are stretched out, the gesture of someone pleading — and there is no one to take them.

Even her neighbours' hostility is traced to the LORD: he commanded it. And she has become a filthy thing among them, the object people step around. The city that was to be a light to the nations is now something they avoid touching.

Verse 18 carries the whole book. In the middle of the worst pain she has ever known, Jerusalem does not accuse God. She accuses herself: for I have rebelled against his word.

That changes everything about how the rest of the book prays. Lamentations is full of raw, loud, honest complaint. But it is the complaint of someone who has first agreed with God about her sin. Paul says the same thing about every human being: Let God be true though every one were a liar (Rom 3:4).

There is a way of suffering that says, "I have done nothing to deserve this," and ends in bitterness. There is another that says, "God is right, and I am hurting, and I am going to tell him both", and that way leads home, because the God who is in the right is the God who forgives the one who confesses (Ps 32:5; 1 John 1:9).

But hear, all you peoples. She asks the nations to learn from her. Her ruin is meant to be a warning (1 Kgs 9:8-9), as the prophets said the same end would come to any people that forsook the LORD.

She called on Egypt, and Egypt did not come (Jer 37:7); her priests and elders died scavenging for food. The idols of security let her down at the moment she needed them.

verseByVerse.quote: "Look, O LORD, for I am in distress; my stomach churns; my heart is wrung within me, because I have been very rebellious. In the street the sword bereaves; in the house it is like death. "They heard my groaning, yet there is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that you have done it. You have brought the day you announced; now let them be as I am. "Let all their evildoing come before you, and deal with them as you have dealt with me because of all my transgressions; for my groans are many, and my heart is faint."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer now turns fully to God, and it is physical: churning stomach, a heart wrung like a cloth. Grief is not only a feeling in the mind. It lives in the body, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so (Ps 31:9-10).

Again the double honesty. I am in distress, and I have been very rebellious. She does not use her pain to excuse her sin, or her sin to silence her pain.

Outside, the sword. Inside, death: famine and disease doing in the houses what the soldiers were doing in the streets. There is nowhere safe to stand.

The ESV notes that the Septuagint and Syriac read "Hear" for They heard, making the line a plea for God to listen. Either way, the fifth and last time: there is no one to comfort me.

The prophets had announced the day for years, and it came. The ESV notes that the Syriac reads "Bring" — a prayer that the LORD will bring the same day on her enemies. And that is what follows: now let them be as I am.

Is this a right prayer? It is not a prayer for private revenge. It asks God to be consistent, to deal with the evil of the nations as he has dealt with the evil of his own people. And God answered it; of Babylon he said, Repay her according to her deeds (Jer 50:29).

Christians pray within the same frame, with more light. We leave vengeance with God (never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, Rom 12:19), and we have heard the one who bore that wrath pray Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34).

And the chapter simply stops, with no resolution and no comforter. Lamentations lets that stand, and so should we when we sit with someone in grief. Do not hurry them to the last page. But know that the comforter she looked for has a name. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4).

1.title: The City with No Comforter
1.overview:
Jerusalem has fallen, and the first poem looks at the ruined city as a widow weeping through the night with no one to comfort her. For the first half of the chapter a narrator describes her (vv. 1-11); for the second, Jerusalem speaks for herself, calling to the passers-by and then to God (vv. 12-22).

Two things are said together and never let go of. The LORD has done this, justly, for the multitude of her transgressions (v. 5), and Jerusalem herself confesses it (v. 18). And the pain is terrible, and is poured out to him without holding back. Five times the refrain sounds, none to comfort her, and the chapter ends without an answer (v. 22). Like chapters 2 and 4, it is an alphabetic poem in Hebrew, grief given the most ordered form the poet has.
1.theology:
The LORD, not Babylon, is the first cause of Jerusalem's ruin, and he acted justly; the covenant curses were fulfilled to the letter (vv. 3, 5, 18; Deut 28:44, 65). Sin defiles as well as condemns, blinds a people to where its road will end, and binds itself together into a yoke too heavy to carry (vv. 8-9, 14; Deut 32:29).

Yet the chapter is also a school of lament. Jerusalem agrees with God about her sin and still pours out her pain to him, asking first only that he would look (vv. 9, 11, 18, 20). That is faith, not unbelief. The comforter she cannot find is the deepest wound of the chapter, and God answers it in Christ, who bore the LORD's anger for the sins of others, and in the Spirit he sends (v. 12; Isa 40:1; Isa 53:5; Matt 27:39; John 14:16-18; 2 Cor 1:3-4).
1.examples:
Anyone who has lain awake after a death knows the picture of verse 2: weeping in the night, when there is nothing to do but feel it, with tears still on the cheeks because no one is there to wipe them away. Lamentations does not tell such a person to cheer up. It gives them words, and turns those words towards God.

The passer-by of verse 12 is also familiar. When a friend's life falls apart, it is easy to walk past their ruin and get on with the day. The church is meant to be the place where no one's sorrow is nothing to anyone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Day of His Anger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second poem looks straight at a hard truth: the ruin was God's own work. How the Lord in his anger has set the daughter of Zion under a cloud! (v. 1). He has swallowed up Jacob without mercy and withdrawn his right hand (vv. 2-4), until the poet says it outright: The Lord has become like an enemy (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's anger is not an impersonal force but the personal opposition of a holy God to sin.

verseByVerse.quote: How the Lord in his anger has set the daughter of Zion under a cloud! He has cast down from heaven to earth the splendor of Israel; he has not remembered his footstool in the day of his anger. The Lord has swallowed up without mercy all the habitations of Jacob; in his wrath he has broken down the strongholds of the daughter of Judah; he has brought down to the ground in dishonor the kingdom and its rulers. He has cut down in fierce anger all the might of Israel; he has withdrawn from them his right hand in the face of the enemy; he has burned like a flaming fire in Jacob, consuming all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 1 kept close to the city and her grief. Chapter 2 turns its eyes to God, and it does not flinch. Count the subjects of the verbs in the first eight verses: nearly every one is the Lord.

Under a cloud. In Israel's story the cloud meant glory — the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Exod 40:34), and at the temple's dedication the priests could not stand to minister because of it (1 Kgs 8:10-11). Now the cloud over Zion is anger.

His footstool is the ark and the temple where it stood, the place where heaven's King rested his feet on earth (1 Chr 28:2; Ps 99:5). The people had assumed God would never let anything happen to his own footstool (Jer 7:4). He did not remember it. No sacred place is a shelter from God for people who will not turn to him.

Without mercy. The phrase returns as without pity (vv. 17, 21), and the whole book turns on the moment the same poet says his mercies never come to an end (3:22). In chapter 2 the mercy is withheld; in chapter 3 the poet finds that it was never exhausted.

Israel had sung of that right hand since the Red Sea: your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy (Exod 15:6). Now the right hand is simply withdrawn, and Judah faces Babylon alone. One of the ways God judges is not to strike but to step back and leave people to what they chose.

verseByVerse.quote: He has bent his bow like an enemy, with his right hand set like a foe; and he has killed all who were delightful in our eyes; in the tent of the daughter of Zion, he has poured out his fury like fire. The Lord has become like an enemy; he has swallowed up Israel; he has swallowed up all its palaces; he has laid in ruins its strongholds, and he has multiplied in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything hangs on the small word like. God has not become a different God, and he has not stopped being in covenant with Israel. But in what he is doing he stands against them exactly as an enemy would — bow bent, arrow aimed.

Modern people often want a God who can be disappointed but never angry. Lamentations will not allow it. God's wrath is not a loss of temper. It is the settled, personal opposition of perfect holiness to evil, and it is the reason Scripture says It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31).

But now bring those words to the cross. Paul says that we were the enemies — while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10). And at the cross the Son himself cried My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). The only way enemies of God become his friends is that God's own Son bore what it is to have God against you. What Jerusalem experienced in part, Jesus drank in full — so that no one who is in him will ever have to say The Lord has become like an enemy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — Festival, Sabbath, King and Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD tears down his own temple and scorns his altar (vv. 6-7), measures the walls for demolition (v. 8), and takes away king, law and vision (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: When a people keeps the forms of worship but refuses the God of the worship, he may take the forms away.

verseByVerse.quote: He has laid waste his booth like a garden, laid in ruins his meeting place; the LORD has made Zion forget festival and Sabbath, and in his fierce indignation has spurned king and priest. The Lord has scorned his altar, disowned his sanctuary; he has delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they raised a clamor in the house of the LORD as on the day of festival.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A booth was a flimsy shelter put up in a vineyard or garden for the harvest season, and torn down when it was over. Isaiah had once pictured the daughter of Zion left like a booth in a vineyard (Isa 1:8). The temple of Solomon, which took seven years to build, came down as easily as a harvest hut.

With it went the whole shape of Israel's life with God: festival and Sabbath, king and priest. The calendar, the throne and the altar were all gifts. Judah had treated them as guarantees.

The temple is loud again — as on the day of festival. But it is the wrong noise: soldiers shouting in triumph where the choirs used to sing.

Why would God scorn his own altar? Because the people had kept up the sacrifices while living in open rebellion. Jeremiah had stood in the temple gate and asked, Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? (Jer 7:11), and centuries later Jesus quoted those words in the temple courts (Matt 21:13). Here is a question for every churchgoer: do I treat worship as a way to meet God, or as insurance against having to obey him?

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line; he did not restrain his hand from destroying; he caused rampart and wall to lament; they languished together. Her gates have sunk into the ground; he has ruined and broken her bars; her king and princes are among the nations; the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision from the LORD. The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence; they have thrown dust on their heads and put on sackcloth; the young women of Jerusalem have bowed their heads to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He stretched out the measuring line. Builders measure before they build; this measuring is for demolition, as careful and deliberate as construction. God had said so through his prophets in Manasseh's day: I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria (2 Kgs 21:13). The fall of the city was not an accident of war. It was determined.

Worse than the broken gates is the silence. The law is no more — no priests left to teach it, no temple to keep it — and her prophets find no vision from the LORD. Amos had warned of a famine... of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), and a psalm that mourns the burning of the sanctuary says there is no longer any prophet (Ps 74:9).

A people that refuses God's word for long enough may find it withdrawn. Do not assume that a Bible on your shelf and a sermon every Sunday will always be there for when you are finally ready to listen. While he still speaks, his word is an open door: Seek the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6).

From the oldest to the youngest, the whole city is on the ground. The elders who used to give counsel at the gate have nothing to say. Sometimes silence and dust are the only honest response, and the church should know how to sit on the ground with the grieving before it knows what to say to them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poet weeps over dying children (vv. 11-13), flattering prophets and mocking enemies (vv. 14-16). But the true explanation is none of these: The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Prophets who hide sin cannot heal, and the God who kept his word in judgment keeps it in mercy too.

verseByVerse.quote: My eyes are spent with weeping; my stomach churns; my bile is poured out to the ground because of the destruction of the daughter of my people, because infants and babies faint in the streets of the city. They cry to their mothers, "Where is bread and wine?" as they faint like a wounded man in the streets of the city, as their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom. What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you, O virgin daughter of Zion? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the narrator's own composure breaks. He has been describing; now he is weeping. It is the voice of the prophet who once said Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears (Jer 9:1).

This matters. The man who most clearly says God did this is also the man most undone by it. There is no coldness in his theology. Anyone who speaks about God's judgment without tears has not understood it. Jesus himself, as he approached the city he knew would be destroyed, saw the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41).

Little children asking the ordinary question they asked every day — and their mothers with nothing to give. They die in their mothers' arms. Sin is never only private; its consequences fall on the most innocent.

If you have lost a child, hear this carefully. The poet does not say these children died for their own sins, or that their mothers failed them; he weeps for them. The God who wrote their cry into Scripture is the God Jesus showed when he took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). The Westminster Confession speaks of elect infants dying in infancy as saved by Christ (Westminster 10.3), and David could say of his dead son, I shall go to him (2 Sam 12:23).

What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? The poet wants to be a comforter, and he cannot find the words; every comparison is too small for a ruin vast as the sea. Who can heal you? is the right question, and there is only one answer. The God who struck is the only one who can heal: For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD (Jer 30:17). And the Healer came in person: with his wounds we are healed (Isa 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Your prophets have seen for you false and deceptive visions; they have not exposed your iniquity to restore your fortunes, but have seen for you oracles that are false and misleading. All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem: "Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?" All your enemies rail against you; they hiss, they gnash their teeth, they cry: "We have swallowed her! Ah, this is the day we longed for; now we have it; we see it!" The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago; he has thrown down without pity; he has made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the might of your foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the tragedy behind the tragedy. The prophets told those who stubbornly followed their own hearts No disaster shall come upon you (Jer 23:17).

They did not expose iniquity to restore your fortunes. Exposing sin would have been the kind thing, because it was the road to restoration. Their smooth words felt like love and ended in famine.

This is a searching verse for every preacher, every parent and every friend. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Prov 27:6). And it is searching for every listener too: people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim 4:3). Which kind of voice do you want in your life?

The city's own songs are thrown back at her. The psalms had called Zion the perfection of beauty (Ps 50:2) and the joy of all the earth (Ps 48:2). Now travellers quote them as a joke.

The gestures are the ones the Gospels record at the cross: those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Mark 15:29; Ps 22:7). The Son of God stood where ruined Jerusalem stood — mocked, apparently abandoned — though he had done nothing to deserve it.

We have swallowed her! The enemies take the credit. But the poet has already said twice who did the swallowing (vv. 2, 5). They think it is their day. It is the LORD's.

Not the false prophets, not the enemy, not chance. The LORD has done what he purposed. The word commanded long ago is the covenant warning of Moses, spelled out in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.

That is terrifying, and it is also the firmest ground of hope in the chapter. A God who keeps his word to the letter in judgment will keep it to the letter in mercy. The same chapter of Leviticus that warned of the siege also said: Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them (Lev 26:44).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Pour Out Your Heart Like Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poet urges the city to weep and pray without rest: Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! (v. 19). And she does, boldly, laying the worst horrors of the siege before him (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fitting response to God's judgment is not silence or flight but prayer that holds nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: Their heart cried to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears stream down like a torrent day and night! Give yourself no rest, your eyes no respite! "Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the night watches! Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children, who faint for hunger at the head of every street."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn comes: Their heart cried to the Lord. The people who had ignored him for so long are now calling on him, and the poet urges them not to stop. Even the city wall is told to weep.

Look where they are told to go with their grief. Not away from God, but before the presence of the Lord, the very Lord who has done this. There is nowhere else to go. The one who wounded is the only one who can bind up (Hos 6:1).

Pour out your heart like water. Water poured out cannot be gathered back and tidied up. That is the kind of prayer God invites: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him (Ps 62:8). You do not need to arrange your feelings before you pray. Bring them as they are.

And pray for the lives of your children. When parents cannot feed their children, cannot protect them, cannot fix what is wrong, they can still lift their hands to God for them. That is not the least a parent can do; it is the most.

verseByVerse.quote: Look, O LORD, and see! With whom have you dealt thus? Should women eat the fruit of their womb, the children of their tender care? Should priest and prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord? In the dust of the streets lie the young and the old; my young women and my young men have fallen by the sword; you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity. You summoned as if to a festival day my terrors on every side, and on the day of the anger of the LORD no one escaped or survived; those whom I held and raised my enemy destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city prays, and the prayer is shocking in its boldness. With whom have you dealt thus? In other words: Lord, these are your people. Remember who we are to you.

That is the argument Moses used on the mountain when God's wrath burned against Israel (Exod 32:11-12). It is not rebellion to remind God of his covenant. It is faith taking hold of the only claim it has.

The horror she names is the one Moses had foretold for a siege: you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters (Deut 28:53). It came true. And priests and prophets were killed in the very sanctuary they had trusted to keep them safe.

You have killed them. She says it to God's face. Scripture includes prayers like this because God would rather have our honest anguish than our polite distance.

Terrors on every side was Jeremiah's own phrase (Jer 6:25), and his enemies once whispered it back at him in mockery (Jer 20:10). Now it has come. God summoned the terrors as people were once summoned to a feast.

The chapter ends with a mother's cry and no answer yet. Jesus, walking to his own death, told the women of Jerusalem do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children (Luke 23:28), because he knew another such day was coming to the city that rejected him. The only shelter from the day of the anger of the LORD is the one who went into that day on our behalf.

Did mothers really eat their children? Yes; it was foretold as the covenant curse (Deut 28:53–57) and had happened in an earlier siege (2 Kgs 6:28–29). Scripture records it to show what sin and judgment truly are, and that God hears the cry even from there.

How should such a verse be read? With tears, and without contempt for those mothers. The poet does not call them monsters; he lays the horror before God as the deepest wound of the siege and asks him to look. For anyone who has seen, suffered or even done unspeakable things under extreme pressure, the verse says that these too may be spoken before the Lord, and that there is a Saviour whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Memories like these should not be carried alone: a pastor, trusted friends and skilled help are part of God's care.

2.title: The Lord Has Become Like an Enemy
2.overview:
The second poem looks at the fall of Jerusalem from God's side: the Lord has become like an enemy (vv. 1-5). He tears down his own temple, rejects king and priest, and withdraws his word (vv. 6-10). The poet weeps over dying children and flattering prophets, yet traces it all to the LORD, who has carried out the word he commanded long ago (vv. 11-17). Then the city pours out her heart before the Lord in bold prayer (vv. 18-22).

Like chapter 1, the poem is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew.
2.theology:
God's wrath is personal: in judgment the Lord acts like an enemy toward his own people (vv. 4-5). His anger is holy, deliberate and measured, not a loss of control (vv. 8, 17; Heb 10:31).

Sacred places and religious forms do not protect people who refuse God himself; he may scorn his own altar (vv. 1, 6-7; Jer 7:4, 11).

God can withdraw his word from those who will not hear it (v. 9; Amos 8:11). Prophets who do not expose sin cannot bring restoration (v. 14; Prov 27:6; 2 Tim 4:3).

The same faithfulness that carried out the covenant curses guarantees the covenant mercy (v. 17; Lev 26:44-45).

The right response to God's judgment is honest, persistent prayer poured out before him, including bold appeal to his covenant relationship (vv. 18-20; Ps 62:8; Exod 32:11-12).

Christ bore God's enmity against sinners so that enemies might be reconciled (Rom 5:10; Matt 27:46), and he wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41).
2.examples:
The cloud of glory turned into a cloud of anger.

A right hand that once shattered enemies, simply withdrawn.

Solomon's temple coming down like a harvest shelter.

A measuring line stretched out for demolition.

A child asking for bread and wine in his mother's arms.

Prophets whose kindness was never to mention sin.

Old songs about Zion quoted back as a joke.

A heart poured out like water that cannot be gathered up again.

Lord, with whom have you dealt thus?
