verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Man Who Has Seen Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man now speaks, and he speaks of God as his attacker. I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath (v. 1). Darkness, chains, unanswered prayer and mockery pile up (vv. 2-17), until he says the bleakest thing he has said: My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer may reach the point of saying his hope is gone — and still be saying it to the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath; he has driven and brought me into darkness without any light; surely against me he turns his hand again and again the whole day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first two poems spoke about a city. Now a single man steps forward, and the whole book narrows to one person's suffering. He does not give his name. His experience is so close to Jeremiah's — mocked by his own people, thrown into a pit — that many have heard the prophet's voice here. But he speaks as someone who carries the nation's grief in his own body, so that anyone who has suffered can stand where he stands. He has seen affliction, lived inside it, under the rod of his wrath.

Darkness is bad enough. Without any light is worse — not a dim room but no lamp at all, no sense of direction, no way to see where the next step goes. Many believers know such a season. Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isa 50:10).

One blow can be survived. What wears a person down is again and again the whole day long — the diagnosis followed by the job loss followed by the family crisis, with no gap to breathe. He feels singled out: against me.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones; he has besieged and enveloped me with bitterness and tribulation; he has made me dwell in darkness like the dead of long ago.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The suffering is physical. Skin, flesh, bones — the famine and siege wrote themselves on the body. Scripture never treats the body as unimportant to God, and it never treats bodily pain as unspiritual.

And yet the God who breaks bones is the God who mends them. David, crushed by his own sin, prayed let the bones that you have broken rejoice (Ps 51:8). The hand that broke is the hand he asked to heal.

An army had walled in Jerusalem; now he says God has done that to him personally — surrounded him with bitterness and tribulation, so that every direction he turns he meets it.

Not just dying but like the dead of long ago — the long-forgotten dead, whom no one visits. A psalmist said the same: You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep (Ps 88:6). That psalm ends in darkness too. God has put such prayers in his book so that no sufferer will ever think his darkness is too dark to bring to God.

verseByVerse.quote: He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer; he has blocked my ways with blocks of stones; he has made my paths crooked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walls and chains: a prisoner with no way out. Job used the same picture — He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass (Job 19:8).

Cruellest of all, he is praying, loudly — I call and cry for help — and it feels as if the prayers hit the ceiling. God shuts out his prayer as someone shuts a door.

Christians sometimes say that God always answers prayer. That is true, but it is not how it always feels, and this verse gives permission to say so. Hold on to this line, though, because at the end of this chapter the same man says you heard my plea (v. 56). The door was not locked forever. And the Son of God, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, and he was heard (Heb 5:7) — so that through him no believer's prayer is ever truly shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding; he turned aside my steps and tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate; he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow. He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the pictures become violent. God is a bear waiting in ambush, a lion crouched in the undergrowth. The man walks into the trap and is torn to pieces.

How can a believer speak of God like this? Because it is honest about how affliction feels, and because the Bible itself uses these images for God's judgment (Hos 5:14). The man is not saying God is cruel. He is saying God is not safe to trifle with — which is exactly what Judah forgot.

Look again at the words tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate. Hosea used that same picture and drew from it a surprising conclusion: Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up (Hos 6:1). A lion tears to kill. God tears to heal. The wound is real, but its purpose is not destruction; it is return.

He feels like the target on an archery range, and every arrow finds its mark, driven deep into the body. Job described the same experience: he set me up as his target; his archers surround me (Job 16:12-13).

You are not the first believer to feel that God has made you his target. And the Son of God, who truly stood under the arrows of God's wrath at the cross, felt it most of all — not for his sins but for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: I have become the laughingstock of all my people, the object of their taunts all day long. He has filled me with bitterness; he has sated me with wormwood. He has made my teeth grind on gravel, and made me cower in ashes;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that some manuscripts read "all peoples." Either way, the mockery is public and constant. But if it is my people, the wound is deeper: those who should have stood with him laugh at him.

Jeremiah knew exactly this: I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me (Jer 20:7). So did Jesus, mocked by the soldiers who knelt before him and cried Hail, King of the Jews! (Matt 27:29).

Wormwood was a plant with an intensely bitter taste, and it became a byword for bitterness in life. To be sated with it is to have eaten nothing else, to have bitterness as your whole diet.

Bread full of grit: every mouthful hurts. And he is made to cower in ashes, pressed down into the ruin of his burned city. Humiliation and pain together.

verseByVerse.quote: my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is; so I say, "My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bereft of peace — peace has been taken from him like a family member taken by death. And I have forgotten what happiness is. The ESV notes that the Hebrew word behind happiness is "good." He has forgotten what good is.

In a few verses the same man will say good three times over (vv. 25-27). He does not remember the good by looking at his circumstances. He relearns it by looking at God.

This is the bottom of the pit. My endurance has perished — I cannot keep going. So has my hope from the LORD — I no longer expect anything from God.

Elijah said something like it under the broom tree: It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life (1 Kgs 19:4).

Yet even at the bottom, he names the LORD. In saying his hope has perished he is still defining his hope by the LORD. A person who has truly let go of God does not grieve the loss of hope in God. The very ache of this verse is a sign that faith is not dead, only exhausted. And the next verses show what exhausted faith does next.

What if this is where I am? Then you are in the company of this man, of Elijah and of the psalmists, and the God who put their words in his book is not ashamed of you. Say it to him as they did. And do not stay there alone: tell a pastor or a trusted friend, and where despair has settled into depression, seek medical help without shame, as you would for any other illness. If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — But This I Call to Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remembering his affliction bows the man down (vv. 19-20). Then he calls something else to mind, the steadfast love and faithfulness of the LORD (vv. 21-23), and finds that when everything else is taken the LORD is still his portion (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Hope in the ruins does not come from the circumstances but from calling to mind the unchanging character of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall! My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He calls on God to remember — the same prayer the whole book prays. My wanderings is the homelessness of exile. The wormwood and the gall are the bitterness again: gall was a byword for poison.

When Jesus hung on the cross, they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, and he would not drink it (Matt 27:34). He refused it. He had come to drink another cup — the bitterness of God's wrath — to the bottom.

Here is the problem with memory. He cannot stop thinking about it, and the more he thinks, the lower he sinks. That is what rumination does: turning the same pain over and over until the soul is bent double.

Many people replay the betrayal, the diagnosis, the loss, night after night. The next verse does not tell him to stop remembering. It tells him what else to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hinge of the whole book. But.

Nothing outside has changed. What has changed is what he is deliberately bringing to mind. This I call to mind — he makes himself remember, the way you might take hold of a railing in the dark.

That is how hope works in Scripture. It is not a mood that comes over you. It is the result of preaching truth to yourself. David did it when his men wanted to stone him: David strengthened himself in the LORD his God (1 Sam 30:6). A psalmist did it: I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old (Ps 77:11). You may not be able to feel your way out of despair, but you can call something to mind, and for the believer the Holy Spirit is the one who does the reminding: he will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (John 14:26). What this man calls to mind is not a technique but a fact about God.

Steadfast love is God's loyal, committed love to his covenant people — the love he proclaimed to Moses when he passed by: a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). It is love that has bound itself by promise and will not let go. John says that in Jesus this God of steadfast love and faithfulness came to live among us, full of grace and truth (John 1:14, 17), and at the cross that love was shown beyond all doubt (Rom 5:8).

The ESV notes that the Hebrew text here reads "Because of the steadfast love of the LORD, we are not cut off," while the ESV follows the Syriac and the Targum. The Hebrew reading is the one the King James Version gives: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed. Both readings stand on the same truth. Either God's love never ceases, or it is the reason we have not ceased. Jerusalem had been struck to the ground — but not wiped out. There were survivors, and there was someone left alive to write this poem. That alone was proof that God's love had not run out.

And set this beside chapter 2, where the Lord swallowed up without mercy (2:2). The mercy had been withheld from the city's walls. It had not been exhausted in God's heart. His mercies never come to an end.

New every morning. Think of the manna in the wilderness: Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat (Exod 16:21). It could not be stored up; each day needed each day's gift. God's mercies are like that. That is why Jesus taught us to pray Give us this day our daily bread (Matt 6:11), and not to be anxious about tomorrow (Matt 6:34).

Some mornings you wake and the weight comes back before you have even opened your eyes. On those mornings, remember that there is a fresh supply of mercy which did not exist last night, and it was made for this morning.

Then he speaks straight to God: great is your faithfulness, now, among the ashes. God's faithfulness is not measured by our circumstances but by his promises, and he keeps them. If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV follows the Syriac and Targum in v. 22 (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD is my portion," says my soul, "therefore I will hope in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A portion was a share of the inheritance, a piece of land to live on and farm. When Israel entered Canaan, every tribe received a portion except one. To the priests God said: You shall have no inheritance in their land... I am your portion and your inheritance (Num 18:20).

Now every Israelite is in that position. The land is lost; chapter 5 will say Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers (5:2). The house, the fields, the temple — gone. And the man says: I still have my portion. The LORD himself.

That is where hope becomes unshakeable. If your portion is your health, your family, your reputation or your savings, it can be taken, and then your hope goes with it. If your portion is the LORD, nothing can take it. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps 73:26).

Says my soul: he is talking to himself again, as in verse 21, and concludes therefore I will hope in him. Not "I feel hopeful" but "I will hope." Hope is a decision made on the basis of who God is.

Christians can say this with more certainty than he could, because God has given us not only himself but his Son. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–39 — It Is Good to Wait Quietly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who had forgotten what good is now says good three times (vv. 25-27). The sufferer waits in humble silence (vv. 28-30), because the Lord does not afflict from his heart (vv. 31-33). He does not approve of injustice, yet nothing happens unless he has commanded it (vv. 34-39).
verseByVerse.theology: God is sovereign over affliction, never cruel in it, and never the approver of the injustice he overrules.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had forgotten what good is (v. 17). Now, in three verses in a row, the word comes back: the LORD is good, it is good to wait, it is good to bear the yoke. The good he could not find in his circumstances he has found in God.

To those who wait for him. Waiting in the Bible is not passive. It is leaning your whole weight on God while nothing seems to happen. And it is paired with the soul who seeks him — waiting is active seeking. They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31).

Quietly. Not without prayer — this book is full of loud prayer — but without the frantic, fretting, grasping panic that tries to force God's hand or find a way out apart from him. In quietness and in trust shall be your strength (Isa 30:15). Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him (Ps 37:7).

A young ox learns to pull by wearing the yoke. It chafes. But an animal that never bore a yoke is useless for the plough. Hard things learned early shape a life: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67).

Some yokes are gifts, for the young and for parents who long to spare them every difficulty. And there is one yoke that every young person should take up as early as possible: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Let him sit alone in silence when it is laid on him; let him put his mouth in the dust— there may yet be hope; let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and let him be filled with insults.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the yoke of affliction is laid on you, the first response is not to argue or to explain it but to sit alone in silence. There is a silence of rebellion, sulking at God. This is the other kind — the silence of someone who has recognised God's hand. I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it (Ps 39:9).

To put your mouth in the dust is to lie face down, as a subject before a king. And there is a quiet line tucked in: there may yet be hope. Not certainty, not a guarantee of how things will turn out, but a door left open. Humility is where hope can begin, because humility stops demanding and starts trusting. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Pet 5:6).

This must be read carefully. The chapter is about accepting God's discipline humbly, not about excusing human cruelty; in a few verses it will say plainly that the Lord does not approve of injustice (vv. 34-36). This verse does not tell anyone to stay in harm's way or to treat abuse as God's will; anyone being abused should seek safety at once. It describes a person who has stopped fighting God, and so no longer needs to hit back at those God uses to humble him.

And here the chapter points straight to Christ. The Servant of the LORD said I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isa 50:6). At his trial, they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67). When he was reviled, he did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). The man in Lamentations gave his cheek because he had sinned. Jesus gave his because we had.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now come three reasons, each beginning for. First, the Lord will not cast off forever. There is an end to discipline, even when you cannot see it. For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Ps 30:5).

The second reason: the grief is real — he cause grief — but compassion follows it, and not a small compassion. It is measured according to the abundance of his steadfast love. The grief has a limit. The love does not.

The third reason goes deepest. God does afflict, and this book has not hidden it for a moment. But he does not afflict from his heart. It is not what he delights in. It is not the centre of who he is.

Ezekiel heard God say the same: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezek 33:11). Isaiah called judgment God's strange deed and alien work (Isa 28:21). Mercy is his heart; judgment is the work his holiness requires when mercy is refused.

When God disciplines his children, he is not enjoying it. He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). A father who must correct his child does it with a heavy heart, and God's heart is heavier and kinder than any father's.

And the proof of what is in God's heart is the cross. There God did the one thing that did come from his heart — he gave his Son out of love — so that his wrath would be satisfied and his compassion could flow freely to sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the earth, to deny a man justice in the presence of the Most High, to subvert a man in his lawsuit, the Lord does not approve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These three verses build to one statement, which comes at the very end: the Lord does not approve. Crushing prisoners, twisting justice in court, cheating someone in a lawsuit — God sees these things and does not approve of any of them.

Why is this here? Because a person who has just said that his suffering comes from God's hand may be tempted to think that everything done to him must therefore be right. It is not. The Babylonians who crushed Judah's prisoners were God's instrument, and they were also guilty. God's sovereignty does not make him the author of anyone's cruelty or the approver of anyone's injustice.

Joseph could say to his brothers you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). Both halves were true. And at the cross the same double truth reached its peak: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and his killers were still lawless men (Acts 2:23).

Note the phrase in the presence of the Most High. Every courtroom on earth sits in the presence of a higher court. Injustice that no human judge corrects is not unseen. For anyone who has been wronged and never had justice, that is solid comfort. For anyone who has done the wronging, it is a solemn warning.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it? Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come? Why should a living man complain, a man, about the punishment of his sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the other side of the truth. God disapproves of injustice, and yet nothing happens outside his command. Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it? Human plans, Babylon's included, come to pass only because God permits and directs them.

And good and bad alike come from the mouth of the Most High. Job said: Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). Isaiah: I make well-being and create calamity (Isa 45:7). The Bible holds this truth without apology, because the alternative is far worse. If there is disaster God does not control, then there is disaster that has no purpose and no end.

This is not a cold doctrine. It is the only thing that makes verse 22 possible. If God controls the bad, then his steadfast love can reach into it, limit it and use it. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

A living man: after everything, he is still breathing, which the Hebrew reading of verse 22 says is itself a mercy. The punishment has been less than the sin.

And complain is not lament. It is the grumbling that accuses God of being unfair. Lament says, "Lord, this hurts; please look." Complaint says, "Lord, I don't deserve this." The man has already admitted that it is the punishment of his sins. So he may lament, and he must not complain.

We may bring every tear to God. But no Christian ever receives what his sins deserve, because Christ received it. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities (Ps 103:10).

Does this mean my own suffering is punishment for my sin? These words speak of Judah’s judgment, announced long before (Deut 28; 2:17). Not all suffering is punishment for a particular sin: Job was blameless, and Jesus said of the blind man It was not that this man sinned (John 9:3). For a believer, Christ bore the punishment of sin (Isa 53:5); hardship may be a Father’s discipline (Heb 12:6), but it is never his condemnation (Rom 8:1). Where we have sinned, the right response is the next verse: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–54 — Let Us Test and Examine Our Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The I becomes we: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD! (v. 40). The people confess their rebellion under a cloud no prayer seems to pass (vv. 41-47), and the speaker weeps until the LORD looks down, remembering the pit where he said I am lost (vv. 48-54).
verseByVerse.theology: Real repentance examines its own ways, confesses without excuse, and keeps praying until God looks down.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD! Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven: "We have transgressed and rebelled, and you have not forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly I becomes us. What is the first thing to do in suffering? Not to examine God's ways but our ways. That is backwards from how most people react. We ask why God allowed this; Lamentations asks what we have done and where we need to turn. It is the prodigal son in the far country: when he came to himself, he said, I will arise and go to my father (Luke 15:17-18).

Examination is not an end in itself. Its purpose is to return to the LORD. Self-examination that stays turned inward becomes morbid. Self-examination that leads to God becomes repentance. Search me, O God, and know my heart!... And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting! (Ps 139:23-24).

Hearts and hands. Lifting hands was the posture of prayer; Judah had lifted hands plenty of times in the temple. What was missing was the heart. Rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:13). God wants the inside to go up with the outside.

The confession is short and makes no excuses. Then an honest, painful line: and you have not forgiven. The exile goes on; they have confessed, and the consequences remain.

That is a hard reality even for Christians: confessing a sin does not always remove its consequences in this life. But the Christian can say something the exiles could not yet say, because Christ has come. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). The consequences may linger. The guilt does not, because Christ's perfect obedience and death are counted as ours: There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). And the same Spirit who brings us back gives us power to walk in new ways (Rom 8:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through. You have made us scum and garbage among the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twice: you have wrapped yourself. First with anger, then with a cloud. The cloud that once filled the temple with glory now blocks prayer like a wall. Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear (Isa 59:2).

Here the gospel speaks with great power. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). The barrier between sinners and God was opened from God's side. Now Christ has entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf (Heb 9:24), and he always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25). For anyone in Christ, there is no cloud that prayer cannot pass through.

The chosen people have become the rubbish of the nations — what everyone else throws away.

The apostle Paul used almost the same words for the life of an apostle: We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things (1 Cor 4:13). But for Paul it was not judgment. It was the privilege of following a Lord who was himself treated as refuse, crucified outside the city like something thrown out. What Judah suffered as the penalty of sin, Christ took on as the price of love, and his people share it as the mark of belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "All our enemies open their mouths against us; panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction; my eyes flow with rivers of tears because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enemies jeer. And the calamity is described in pairs that pile on each other: panic and pitfall, devastation and destruction. Terror on the inside, traps on the outside, ruin all around.

The speaker's tears are now rivers, and they are for the daughter of my people: personal pain has become grief for others. Pain can shrink us so that we can see nothing but ourselves. Or it can enlarge us so that we weep with those who weep. Jesus, riding into the city where he would die, wept over it (Luke 19:41).

verseByVerse.quote: "My eyes will flow without ceasing, without respite, until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees; my eyes cause me grief at the fate of all the daughters of my city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will not stop weeping, and he will not stop praying, until God looks. Isaiah prayed the same: Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation (Isa 63:15). Jesus told a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). There are prayers that need to be prayed many times, for many years, until the Lord looks down. Do not stop praying them.

What he sees makes him weep. He has watched the young women of Jerusalem suffer (1:4, 18; 2:21), and the memory of their faces does not leave him. Grief for others is not weakness. It is a heart like God's.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have been hunted like a bird by those who were my enemies without cause; they flung me alive into the pit and cast stones on me; water closed over my head; I said, 'I am lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was hunted like a bird by enemies without cause; he had done them no wrong.

That phrase echoes through the psalms: without cause they dug a pit for my life (Ps 35:7). Jesus took it up for himself: They hated me without a cause (John 15:25). The righteous sufferer who is hated for no reason finds his fullest meaning in Christ.

Thrown into a pit alive, with stones thrown down on top. The ESV notes that the line may be rendered "they end my life in the pit" — they meant him to die there.

It is hard not to think of Jeremiah, whose enemies cast him into the cistern where there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud (Jer 38:6), expecting him to die there of hunger (Jer 38:9).

Jonah said something very like it: The waters closed in over me to take my life (Jonah 2:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 55–66 — You Came Near When I Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the pit he called, and the LORD came near and redeemed his life (vv. 55-58). He asks God to judge his cause and commits his enemies to the LORD's justice (vv. 59-66).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who seemed to shut out prayer is the God who comes near, speaks peace and redeems.

verseByVerse.quote: "I called on your name, O LORD, from the depths of the pit; you heard my plea, 'Do not close your ear to my cry for help!' You came near when I called on you; you said, 'Do not fear!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the very bottom — the depths of the pit — he called on the LORD. No one can fall so far that he is out of calling distance. Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD! (Ps 130:1).

Remember verse 8: though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer. And verse 44: no prayer can pass through. Now: you heard my plea. What felt like a locked door was not locked forever. For anyone praying through the silence, how it feels now is not the last word on whether God hears.

God, who had seemed like a bear and a lion and an archer, comes near and says Do not fear!

That is the word God speaks again and again to his frightened people: fear not, for I am with you (Isa 41:10). It is the word Jesus spoke on the stormy lake: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Matt 14:27). And it is the word the risen Christ spoke to John, who fell at his feet as though dead: Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore (Rev 1:17-18). The God who comes near to the man in the pit came near to us in person, went down into the pit of death himself, and came back up.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life. You have seen the wrong done to me, O LORD; judge my cause. You have seen all their vengeance, all their plots against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two legal pictures. You have taken up my cause — God has become his advocate in court. You have redeemed my life — God has paid to set him free, like a family member buying back a relative sold into slavery.

Jeremiah had promised exactly this for the exiles: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause (Jer 50:34).

And the New Testament shows how far this goes. If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). Our advocate does not only plead our case; he paid our debt. He is both the lawyer and the ransom.

The prayer of chapter 1 was Look, O LORD, and see. Now he knows God has seen. Nothing done in secret against God's people is hidden from him.

So he asks God to judge my cause. He does not take justice into his own hands. He hands his case to the one Judge who sees everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard their taunts, O LORD, all their plots against me. The lips and thoughts of my assailants are against me all the day long. Behold their sitting and their rising; I am the object of their taunts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seen (vv. 59-60), and now heard: God knows the enemies' lips and thoughts.

Their sitting and their rising means everything they do from morning to night. Whether they sit down or get up, they are mocking him. You know when I sit down and when I rise up (Ps 139:2) — the God who knows every movement of his own people also knows every movement of their enemies.

If you are being slandered, mocked or plotted against, this is where to take it. Not into a counter-campaign, but to the God who has seen, and heard, and knows.

verseByVerse.quote: "You will repay them, O LORD, according to the work of their hands. You will give them dullness of heart; your curse will be on them. You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under your heavens, O LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ESV notes that each of these lines can be read as a prayer rather than a statement: "Repay them," "Give them," "Pursue them" — and "place your curse" for your curse will be on them. The man is either declaring what God will do or asking him to do it. Either way he is leaving it with God.

And what he asks is simply justice: according to the work of their hands. Not more than they deserve. The Bible never tells believers to pretend that evil does not matter. God himself considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you (2 Thess 1:6).

Dullness of heart is a heart that can no longer take in the truth. It is a judgment God pronounced through Isaiah on a people who would not listen: Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes (Isa 6:10). There is something more fearful than pain: a heart that no longer hears God. It is also a reason to pray, while the heart can still hear, for those who have not yet turned.

And listen to You will pursue them in anger. Earlier the people had said to God, You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us (v. 43). The prayer asks God to do to Babylon what he has done to Judah, as Zion had asked in the first poem (1:22). God's justice has no favourites. If his own people did not escape it, their oppressors will not either.

But see where the vengeance is placed: in God's hands, not the man's. That is exactly the New Testament command: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). A believer who has truly handed justice over to God is free — free from bitterness, free to forgive, even free to pray for his enemies, as Jesus did on the cross (Luke 23:34). For the enemy who repents, Christ has already borne the curse (Gal 3:13).

The chapter's last words are from under your heavens, O LORD. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "the heavens of the LORD." The chapter that began in darkness ends looking up at the LORD's heavens, from which he waited for God to look down (v. 50). He has not yet seen the end, but he has seen God come near, and that is enough to wait on.

3.title: His Mercies Are New Every Morning
3.overview:
Lamentations 3 is the heart of the book. One man speaks of God as his attacker until he says his hope from the LORD is gone (vv. 1-18). Then he calls to mind the steadfast love and new mercies of the LORD, his portion (vv. 19-24), and teaches what he has learned about waiting quietly under God's hand (vv. 25-39). The I becomes we as the people are called to examine their ways and return (vv. 40-54), and the chapter ends with the LORD coming near to the man in the pit (vv. 55-66).

In Hebrew the chapter is an alphabetic poem in sets of three: sixty-six verses, three for each letter of the alphabet.
3.theology:
A believer may say his hope is gone and still be speaking to the LORD (v. 18); hope returns by calling to mind the character of God (v. 21). The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases, and his mercies are new every morning; his faithfulness is great even among the ashes (vv. 22-23; Exod 34:6; 2 Tim 2:13). When every earthly portion is lost, the LORD himself remains the portion of his people (v. 24; Num 18:20; Ps 73:26).

Affliction is ordained by God, yet it does not come from his heart; compassion according to his abundant steadfast love always follows grief for his people (vv. 31-33; Ezek 33:11; Heb 12:10).

God is sovereign over good and bad alike, yet he never approves of human injustice; the instruments of his judgment remain guilty (vv. 34-38; Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23).

Lament is right; complaint against God's justice is not (v. 39). True repentance examines its own ways and confesses without excuse (vv. 40-42).

God hears prayer from the depths, comes near, and says Do not fear; he is his people's advocate and redeemer (vv. 55-58; Jer 50:34). In Christ the barrier to prayer is torn away, and the believer has an advocate who also paid the ransom (Matt 27:51; Heb 7:25; 1 John 2:1).

Justice against enemies belongs to God, and leaving it with him sets the believer free to forgive (vv. 64-66; Rom 12:19; Luke 23:34).

The man of affliction points beyond himself to Christ, who suffered not for his own sins but for ours (vv. 14, 30, 52-53; Isa 50:6; John 15:25; 1 Pet 2:23).
3.examples:
Darkness without any light.

A prayer that feels like it hits the ceiling.

Bread full of gravel.

A man who has forgotten what good is.

Replaying the same pain night after night.

But this I call to mind — taking hold of a railing in the dark.

Manna gathered morning by morning; mercy that cannot be stored up.

Losing the land and discovering that your portion is the LORD.

A young ox learning to pull.

A mouth in the dust, and a door left open: there may yet be hope.

A Father who corrects with a heavy heart.

The curtain torn from top to bottom.

A man at the bottom of a cistern, calling.

You came near; you said, Do not fear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fourth poem returns to the siege and looks at what it did to people. How the gold has grown dim, how the pure gold is changed! (v. 1). The precious sons of Zion are treated like clay pots (v. 2), children starve and princes shrivel (vv. 3-8), and the punishment is heavier than Sodom's (v. 6), down to the worst horror of the siege (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin does not only bring punishment; it strips a people of the dignity and tenderness God gave them.

verseByVerse.quote: How the gold has grown dim, how the pure gold is changed! The holy stones lie scattered at the head of every street. The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poem opens with the same cry as chapters 1 and 2 — How — and a picture of treasure ruined. Pure gold does not tarnish; yet this gold has grown dim. Holy stones lie in the gutters. The next verse shows that he is mourning not the temple treasury but people.

Earthen pots were the cheapest things in a household — used, cracked and thrown on the rubbish heap. The young men of Jerusalem, precious as gold, are now treated as disposable.

Two questions come out of this verse. First: where does a person's worth come from? Not from how others treat him. God said to his people, you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you (Isa 43:4). Their value did not change when Babylon despised them.

Second: the picture of clay pots is Jeremiah's own (Jer 18-19), and the apostle takes it up with a twist of glory. We have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Cor 4:7). The world may regard God's people as earthen pots. God has filled them with treasure — and paid for them, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: Even jackals offer the breast; they nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. The tongue of the nursing infant sticks to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children beg for food, but no one gives to them. Those who once feasted on delicacies perish in the streets; those who were brought up in purple embrace ash heaps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jackals were despised scavengers. Yet even jackals feed their young. In the book of Job the ostrich is the careless mother: she leaves her eggs to the earth... She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers (Job 39:14, 16).

Famine has done something worse than kill: it has hardened hearts. Sin's consequences reach down into the most natural affections God created.

No one gives to them, not because no one loves them, but because no one has anything left (compare 2:11-12). Purple was the colour of royalty and wealth. Children raised in the best homes of Jerusalem now cling to rubbish heaps, looking for anything to eat.

Jesus told of a rich man clothed in purple who feasted every day while a beggar lay at his gate, and of the reversal that came: you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish (Luke 16:19, 25). Wealth is no protection on the day God overturns things. The only safe way to be rich is to be rich toward God (Luke 12:21).

verseByVerse.quote: For the chastisement of the daughter of my people has been greater than the punishment of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and no hands were wrung for her. Her princes were purer than snow, whiter than milk; their bodies were more ruddy than coral, the beauty of their form was like sapphire. Now their face is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as wood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sodom was destroyed in a moment. Jerusalem's agony went on and on through a long siege and a slow famine. In that sense her suffering was greater.

The ESV notes also point to a deeper reading: chastisement can be rendered "iniquity" and punishment "sin." Then the verse says the iniquity of Jerusalem was greater than the sin of Sodom. Ezekiel said exactly that: your sister Sodom and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done (Ezek 16:48).

How could that be? Because Jerusalem had received what Sodom never had — the law, the temple, the prophets, the covenant. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48). Jesus said the same to the towns where he had worked his miracles: it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you (Matt 11:24).

For anyone who has grown up with the Bible, privilege does not shelter from judgment; it raises the stakes. Yet the same Jesus who warned those towns went on to say, Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden (Matt 11:28). (The ESV notes that the meaning of the last line, no hands were wrung for her, is uncertain.)

The young nobles had been the picture of health and beauty. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind sapphire is "lapis lazuli," a deep blue stone, and that the meaning of the beauty of their form is uncertain.) Now their own neighbours do not recognise them.

Human beauty and strength are real gifts, and they are fragile. Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). And there was one whose appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance (Isa 52:14), not because of his sin but so that ours could be dealt with.

verseByVerse.quote: Happier were the victims of the sword than the victims of hunger, who wasted away, pierced by lack of the fruits of the field. The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children; they became their food during the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death by the sword was quick; death by famine was slow, pierced not by a blade but by hunger.

Compassionate women, not monsters, were driven by starvation to eat their own children.

Moses had warned of exactly this, in almost unbearable detail: The most tender and refined woman among you... will eat them secretly, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in your towns (Deut 28:56-57). It had happened once before, in the siege of Samaria (2 Kgs 6:28-29).

The word compassionate will not let the reader despise these women. Their tenderness is the measure of how terrible the siege was, and the poem grieves for them as well as for their children. The one who later longed over this same city as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (Matt 23:37) is not without pity for mothers broken by its fall.

Why does God let such things be recorded? Because we need to know what sin really is and where it leads when God finally gives a people over to it. Sin is not a small thing that God overlooks. A nation's long rebellion, and the siege it brought, can unravel everything good he made, down to a mother's love. And only when we see that clearly do we understand why the cross had to be so terrible, and why grace is so amazing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — For the Sins of Her Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD gave full vent to his wrath, though no one believed Jerusalem could fall (vv. 11-12). The reason lies with her prophets and priests (v. 13), who now wander defiled, driven off like lepers (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who lead God's people bear the heaviest responsibility, and the judgment fell hard on the leaders.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD gave full vent to his wrath; he poured out his hot anger, and he kindled a fire in Zion that consumed its foundations. The kings of the earth did not believe, nor any of the inhabitants of the world, that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Full vent: for centuries God had been slow to anger, sending prophet after prophet. Now the anger is poured out, and the fire reaches the foundations. Moses had sung of it: a fire is kindled by my anger... and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains (Deut 32:22).

There is another place where God's wrath was given full vent, and it is the one that matters most. At the cross, God put his Son forward as a propitiation by his blood (Rom 3:25) — the sacrifice that bears and turns away wrath. Jerusalem's fire burned for a season and left survivors. The wrath that fell on Christ was spent in full, so that for those who trust him none is left over.

Jerusalem had withstood the Assyrians in Hezekiah's day, and everyone assumed it could not fall — its own people most of all (Jer 7:4).

No city, no church, no nation and no person is too established to fall if it abandons God. The sense of being untouchable is itself one of the signs of danger.

verseByVerse.quote: This was for the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in the midst of her the blood of the righteous. They wandered, blind, through the streets; they were so defiled with blood that no one was able to touch their garments. "Away! Unclean!" people cried at them. "Away! Away! Do not touch!" So they became fugitives and wanderers; people said among the nations, "They shall stay with us no longer." The LORD himself has scattered them; he will regard them no more; no honor was shown to the priests, no favor to the elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the poet names the root. The people whose job was to speak for God and to lead worship had become the chief offenders.

And they had shed... the blood of the righteous. Jeremiah himself was nearly killed by them: the priests and the prophets and all the people laid hold of him, saying, "You shall die!" (Jer 26:8).

Jesus stood in the same city six centuries later and spoke to its religious leaders about all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt 23:35). Within days, the priests had handed over the Righteous One himself. Religious leaders have a unique power to do harm, because they do it in God's name. That is why Scripture judges them so strictly — and why every pastor and teacher should tremble.

The men who had pronounced others unclean are now treated as unclean themselves. The law required a leper to cry out, 'Unclean, unclean' and to live alone outside the camp (Lev 13:45-46). Now the priests and prophets are driven off with that cry.

When a leper knelt before Jesus, he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:41). And Jesus himself suffered outside the gate, driven out like an unclean thing, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb 13:12). The Holy One made himself the outcast so that outcasts could be made clean.

The ESV notes that where it reads The LORD himself, the Hebrew says "The face of the LORD." That is a heartbreaking phrase for a priest to hear. The priests had been commanded to bless the people with the words the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you (Num 6:25). Now the face of the LORD has scattered them.

And yet the gospel brings that blessing back to people who had lost it: God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–20 — A Nation Which Could Not Save
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people watched in vain for a nation that could not save them, while the hunters closed in (vv. 17-19), and the last hope, the LORD's anointed king, was captured (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Every saviour but God fails at the moment he is needed, even the king of David's line.

verseByVerse.quote: Our eyes failed, ever watching vainly for help; in our watching we watched for a nation which could not save. They dogged our steps so that we could not walk in our streets; our end drew near; our days were numbered, for our end had come. Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles in the heavens; they chased us on the mountains; they lay in wait for us in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
During the siege the people watched the horizon for help, above all from Egypt. An Egyptian army did march out, and then it went home (Jer 37:7). They watched until their eyes gave out, for a nation which could not save.

Every one of us has an Egypt: the thing we look to for rescue instead of God. A relationship, a career, a savings account, a political leader, a medical treatment. Some of these are good gifts. None of them can save. Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation (Ps 146:3). There is salvation in no one else but Christ (Acts 4:12).

Moses had warned of a nation swooping down like the eagle (Deut 28:49); Jeremiah said his horses are swifter than eagles (Jer 4:13). When the wall was breached and the king and soldiers fled by night toward the Arabah, the Babylonians caught them in the plains of Jericho (Jer 39:4-5). There was nowhere to run from a judgment God had sent.

verseByVerse.quote: The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed, was captured in their pits, of whom we said, "Under his shadow we shall live among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is King Zedekiah, the last king of David's line to reign in Jerusalem. The Babylonians captured the king, killed his sons before his eyes, blinded him and took him to Babylon in chains (2 Kgs 25:6-7).

The people had called him the breath of our nostrils, as necessary as air, and their shelter. Zedekiah was a weak and faithless king, but he sat on David's throne, and God had promised that David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne (Jer 33:17). When he was dragged off, it looked as though God's promise to David had died with him.

It had not. Jeremiah had spoken of a coming righteous Branch for David, whose name would be The LORD is our righteousness (Jer 23:5-6).

And the New Testament shows the shape of the fulfilment. The psalm had said The kings of the earth set themselves... against the LORD and against his Anointed (Ps 2:2), and the apostles saw it happen in Jerusalem, where Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed (Acts 4:26-27). The true Anointed was also captured. He too was handed over to foreign rulers. But he rose, and he reigns. Zedekiah could not give his people a shadow to live under. Christ can: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty (Ps 91:1).
verseByVerse.note: “The LORD’s anointed” is King Zedekiah, captured as he fled.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom, who gloated over Jerusalem's fall, is told to rejoice while it can: to you also the cup shall pass (v. 21). And for the first time since chapter 3 a clear word of hope is spoken to Zion (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The cup of wrath does not stay with God's people forever; for them the punishment has an end.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz; but to you also the cup shall pass; you shall become drunk and strip yourself bare. The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished; he will keep you in exile no longer; but your iniquity, O daughter of Edom, he will punish; he will uncover your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom was Israel's brother nation, descended from Esau (Gen 25:30). When Jerusalem fell, Edom cheered and helped. The psalmist remembered: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!" (Ps 137:7). Obadiah condemned it: do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune (Obad 12).

Rejoice and be glad is bitter irony. To you also the cup shall pass. The cup of God's wrath, which Jeremiah had been told to make the nations drink — Edom named among them (Jer 25:15, 21) — will come round to Edom too. As you have done, it shall be done to you (Obad 15).

No one should gloat over another's fall under God's judgment. The same cup is passed around the whole world. The only question is whether someone else has drunk it for you.

And then, suddenly, a word of hope: the punishment is accomplished. It will not go on forever. The ESV notes that the next line may also be read "he will not exile you again."

It is the same message God had given through Isaiah: cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned (Isa 40:2). And it points beyond the return from Babylon to a greater completion. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed let this cup pass from me (Matt 26:39), and then he drank it. On the cross he said It is finished (John 19:30).

Here are the two destinies of the whole human race. For Zion, the punishment is accomplished. For Edom, the sins are uncovered. The difference is not how bad Zion had been; on one reading of verse 6 her iniquity was greater than Sodom's. The difference is that God had bound himself to her by covenant, and in Christ he binds himself to everyone who comes to him.
verseByVerse.note: Uz here is linked with Edom, which gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.

4.title: How the Gold Has Grown Dim
4.overview: The fourth poem goes back to the siege and looks at what it did to people: the precious sons of Zion treated like clay pots, children starving, mothers broken (vv. 1-10). The poet names the root in the sins of her prophets and priests (vv. 11-16). The people recall watching in vain for a nation that could not save, and the capture of the LORD's anointed king (vv. 17-20). Edom will drink the cup in turn, and to Zion comes the first clear word of hope since chapter 3: the punishment of your iniquity is accomplished (vv. 21-22). Like chapters 1 and 2, the poem is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew.
4.theology:
A person's worth before God does not change when the world treats him as worthless (vv. 1-2; Isa 43:4; 1 Pet 1:18-19).

Sin's consequences reach into the most natural affections God created, even a mother's love; the covenant curses were fulfilled exactly as Moses warned (vv. 3-4, 10; Deut 28:56-57).

Greater privilege brings greater accountability: Jerusalem's judgment exceeded Sodom's (v. 6; Ezek 16:48; Matt 11:23-24; Luke 12:48).

Religious leaders who abuse their office and silence the righteous bear heavy guilt (v. 13; Jer 26:8; Matt 23:35).

Every saviour other than God fails, whether foreign allies or a king of David's line (vv. 17, 20; Ps 146:3). God's promise to David did not die with Zedekiah; it was fulfilled in Jesus, the Anointed who was captured and rose (Jer 23:5-6; Acts 4:26-27).

The cup of wrath passes to every nation, but for God's covenant people the punishment has an end. In Christ it has been fully borne: it is finished (vv. 21-22; Isa 40:2; Matt 26:39; John 19:30).
4.examples:
Pure gold that has somehow tarnished.

Young men worth their weight in gold, treated like cheap clay pots.

A jackal that feeds her young when a mother cannot.

Children in purple, clinging to a rubbish heap.

Neighbours who no longer recognise each other's faces.

Priests who once pronounced others unclean, driven off with the cry: Unclean!

Watching the horizon for an army that turned back.

The breath of our nostrils, dragged away in chains.

Your punishment is accomplished.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace!<sup>2</sup>Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our homes to foreigners.<sup>3</sup>We have become orphans, fatherless; our mothers are like widows.<sup>4</sup>We must pay for the water we drink; the wood we get must be bought.<sup>5</sup>Our pursuers are at our necks; we are weary; we are given no rest.<sup>6</sup>We have given the hand to Egypt, and to Assyria, to get bread enough.<sup>7</sup>Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities.<sup>8</sup>Slaves rule over us; there is none to deliver us from their hand.<sup>9</sup>We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness.<sup>10</sup>Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine.<sup>11</sup>Women are raped in Zion, young women in the towns of Judah.<sup>12</sup>Princes are hung up by their hands; no respect is shown to the elders.<sup>13</sup>Young men are compelled to grind at the mill, and boys stagger under loads of wood.<sup>14</sup>The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music.<sup>15</sup>The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning.<sup>16</sup>The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned!<sup>17</sup>For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim,<sup>18</sup>for Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it.<sup>19</sup>But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.<sup>20</sup>Why do you forget us forever, why do you forsake us for so many days?<sup>21</sup>Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old—<sup>22</sup>unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Look, and See Our Disgrace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last poem is a prayer from the whole community: Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace! (v. 1). Then they list what occupation has meant, from lost land and paid-for water to famine and their fathers' sins (vv. 2-10).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people may bring the concrete details of their distress to him and ask him to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace! Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our homes to foreigners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last poem begins with a prayer, and it is spoken by everyone: from the first verse to the last it is we, us, our.

Remember. When the Bible asks God to remember, it is not reminding him of something he has forgotten. It is asking him to act on what he knows. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen 8:1). God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant, and the exodus began (Exod 2:24).

A dying thief made the same prayer beside Jesus: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42). He was heard that very day (Luke 23:43).

The land had never been Israel's to sell. God said the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev 25:23). Now the inheritance he gave, family by family, has been handed over to others.

Christians are given a different inheritance, one that cannot be turned over to strangers: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:4). Houses can be lost. What God keeps for his people cannot.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 5 has 22 verses but is not an acrostic: a prayer rather than a lament.

verseByVerse.quote: We have become orphans, fatherless; our mothers are like widows. We must pay for the water we drink; the wood we get must be bought. Our pursuers are at our necks; we are weary; we are given no rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many men dead or in exile, the families left behind had no one to protect them. Yet God calls himself Father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Ps 68:5). Jesus, the night before he died, said to his friends, I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you (John 14:18). No one who belongs to Christ is ever truly an orphan.

Water from their own wells and wood from their own hills now had to be bought from the occupiers.

Set it beside what God had given them at the beginning: cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant (Deut 6:11). They had received everything free and treated it as theirs by right. Now they paid for water. And set it beside what God offers still: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isa 55:1). Sin makes us pay for what grace gives away.

They are tired, and no one lets them stop: the curse Moses had described: among these nations you shall find no respite (Deut 28:65).

Weariness without rest is a picture of life under sin. And the one who can end it has said: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: We have given the hand to Egypt, and to Assyria, to get bread enough. Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities. Slaves rule over us; there is none to deliver us from their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give the hand was to make a pact or to submit. For years Judah had turned to Egypt and Assyria for security, and Jeremiah had asked, what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? (Jer 2:18). Now they hold out their hands to foreign powers simply to eat.

Every soul goes looking for bread somewhere. Only one place gives enough: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

It is true that sin's consequences pass down the generations. God himself said he visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children (Exod 34:7). The generation that caused the ruin was mostly dead, and their children were living in it.

But read on to verse 16: woe to us, for we have sinned! The people do not hide behind their fathers. They carry consequences they did not start, and they also confess sins they have committed themselves. Ezekiel had to correct the exiles who used the first truth to deny the second (Ezek 18:2-4).

Both halves are true for us too. We inherit damage from those who came before us, and we are responsible for our own sin. And the gospel answers both: of the Servant of the LORD it is said, he shall bear their iniquities (Isa 53:11). The iniquities we inherited and the iniquities we added, he carried.

Servants of a foreign power now order them about, and there is none to deliver. That is also the condition of every person under sin. Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin — and the slave cannot free himself. But the next words are the gospel: So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34, 36).

verseByVerse.quote: We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness. Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going out to gather food meant risking raiders in the open country. Every meal cost a risk to someone's life.

Prayer like this is not unspiritual. God invites his people to tell him exactly what is wrong — the price of water, the danger of the fields, the fever in the body. Give us this day our daily bread (Matt 6:11) is a prayer Jesus taught. Nothing that concerns your life is too ordinary to bring to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer names the worst of it (vv. 11-15). Then the confession: The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned! (v. 16). Zion's desolation makes them heartsick (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind every loss the people come back to the one cause they can confess: we have sinned.

verseByVerse.quote: Women are raped in Zion, young women in the towns of Judah. Princes are hung up by their hands; no respect is shown to the elders. Young men are compelled to grind at the mill, and boys stagger under loads of wood. The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bible names this and does not look away. Rape was, and still is, a weapon of war. That the verse stands in Scripture matters for every woman who has suffered this. God has seen it. He has written it into his own book as an outrage. It is not hidden from him and it is not unimportant to him. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Ps 34:18). And the church, which carries this book, must be a place where such suffering can be spoken of and is met with compassion, not silence. If this has happened to you, it was not your fault and the shame is not yours; seek safety and help, and tell someone you trust.

The old men, whom the law commanded to be honoured — You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man (Lev 19:32) — are treated with contempt.

The law said a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut 21:23). The princes of Judah were hung up in public disgrace, and Paul quotes that law when he explains the cross: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The Prince of Peace was hung up too, so that the curse on his people could end.

Grinding grain was the work of servants and prisoners. When the Philistines captured Samson, he ground at the mill in the prison (Judg 16:21). The strength of Judah's young men is being spent in slave labour, and even boys are loaded down like pack animals.

The gate was where the elders sat to settle disputes and give counsel; now no one sits there. The young men used to play music; now there is none. Wisdom and joy have both gone out of the city.

verseByVerse.quote: The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning. The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned! For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim, for Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the exact reverse of the psalm: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing (Ps 30:11). Sin turned dancing into mourning. Only God can turn it back.

And he promised to. Through Jeremiah he had already said: Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy (Jer 31:13). The very losses in these verses — young women, young men, the old, dancing, joy — are the ones God named in his promise.

The crown, their glory as God's people, lies in the dust. And here, at last, is the reason: after all the lament, the prayer comes back to the heart of the matter. No blaming Babylon, no blaming the fathers: we have sinned.

That is where every road back to God begins. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13). And the one who wore a crown of thorns gives his people a crown that cannot fall: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life (Rev 2:10).

Of all the losses, this one makes them heartsick: Mount Zion, where God put his name, is desolate. Jeremiah had said God would make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals (Jer 9:11). Now wild animals walk where the priests used to minister.

What they grieve most is not their comfort but the place of God's presence. That is a good test of any heart: what grieves you most? But there is comfort here too. The New Testament tells believers you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). The Zion that jackals prowl was never the final one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — But You, O LORD, Reign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything on earth has fallen, but one throne has not: But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations (v. 19). So the people dare to ask why he has forgotten them (v. 20), pray to be restored to him (v. 21), and end on an open fear (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends on a question only God can answer, and his answer is that he does not utterly reject his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you. Everything in the first eighteen verses has fallen, and here the prayer looks up. David's throne in Jerusalem is gone. The LORD's throne is not. But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations (Ps 102:12). The collapse of every earthly throne does not touch the throne of heaven.

That is the ground under everything else. If God still reigns, then what happened was not beyond his control, and what comes next is not beyond his power.

And the New Testament shows whose throne it is. Of the Son he says, "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" (Heb 1:8). At the end of the Bible, in the new Jerusalem, stands the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:3). The throne that endures to all generations belongs to the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you forget us forever, why do you forsake us for so many days? Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old— unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God reigns forever, the question becomes sharper, not softer: then why? If you are King, why have you left us so long? This is the language of the psalms: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps 13:1).

God had already answered this question through Isaiah. Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me." And God replied: Can a woman forget her nursing child...? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (Isa 49:14-16).

And there was one who was truly forsaken. On the cross Jesus cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). He was forsaken so that God could say to all who are in him: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

Restore us to yourself: not first to the land, not first to prosperity, but to God. The deepest loss was never the city. It was God.

And that we may be restored. They know they cannot turn themselves around. If they are to come back, God must bring them back. It is Ephraim's prayer in Jeremiah: bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God (Jer 31:18), and the psalm's: Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved! (Ps 80:3).

This is the heart of grace. Repentance is something we do, and it is also something God gives, by the Spirit who gives a new heart (Ezek 36:26). No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). If you want to come back to God and find you cannot make your heart do it, pray this prayer. It is the prayer he answers.

Renew our days as of old. Not simply turn the clock back, but make new. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17).

And so the book ends not with an answer but with a fear: unless. This is deliberate. Lamentations does not tie a bow on grief. It leaves the question hanging, because that is how grief really feels, and because the answer does not lie in the people's feelings. It lies in God. (When the book is read in the synagogue, verse 21 is read again after verse 22, so that the reading does not end on that fear.)

And God had already answered. I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them (Lev 26:44). If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel (Jer 31:37). Paul asked the same question centuries later: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Rom 11:1).

The final answer is a person. Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected (Mark 8:31). He was utterly rejected. He bore the exceeding anger of God. And because he did, he can make a promise that closes the question at the end of Lamentations for everyone who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

5.title: Remember, O LORD
5.overview: The last poem of Lamentations is a prayer from the whole community. It asks the LORD to remember and lays before him what life under occupation has become (vv. 1-10), names the worst of it and confesses we have sinned (vv. 11-18), and then looks up to the LORD who reigns forever, asking him to restore them to himself (vv. 19-22). The poem has twenty-two verses like the acrostics before it, but it does not follow the alphabet, and the book ends with its question still open.
5.theology:
To ask God to remember is to ask him to act on his covenant (v. 1; Gen 8:1; Exod 2:24; Luke 23:42). God's people may bring every concrete detail of their suffering to him (vv. 2-18).

Sin's consequences pass down the generations, yet each generation must confess its own sin; the Servant of the LORD bears both (vv. 7, 16; Exod 34:7; Ezek 18:2-4; Isa 53:11).

Scripture does not hide the violence done to the weak; God sees it and records it as an outrage (vv. 11-13; Ps 34:18).

When every earthly throne falls, the LORD's throne endures, and it is the throne of God and of the Lamb (v. 19; Ps 102:12; Heb 1:8; Rev 22:3).

Restoration is first restoration to God himself, and it is God's gift: he must turn his people if they are to be turned (v. 21; Jer 31:18; Ps 80:3; John 6:44).

God does not utterly reject his people (v. 22; Lev 26:44; Jer 31:37; Rom 11:1-2). Christ was rejected so that no one who comes to him will ever be cast out (Mark 8:31; John 6:37).
5.examples:
Paying for water from your own well.

Other families living in the houses your grandparents built.

Holding out your hand to a foreign power for a loaf.

An empty city gate and no music.

A crown in the dust, and the words: we have sinned.

Jackals walking where the priests once ministered.

But you, O LORD, reign forever.

A prayer to be turned by a people who cannot turn themselves.

A book that ends with unless — and a Saviour who answers it.
